stem: A project's single CLAUDE.md has grown past 200 lines covering naming, testing, deployment, API design, and infrastructure. Most maintainable way to reorganize it?

options.label: A
options.body: Move topic-specific conventions into `.claude/rules/` files (testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md).
options.rationale: Correct. `.claude/rules/` is the designed mechanism for splitting conventions by topic — each file handles one concern.

options.label: B
options.body: Split it into multiple CLAUDE.md files in the root directory.
options.rationale: You can't have multiple CLAUDE.md files in the same directory; `.claude/rules/` is the split mechanism.

options.label: C
options.body: Move everything to user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so each developer customizes.
options.rationale: User-level config isn't shared via git — new team members would get nothing.

options.label: D
options.body: Create a skill that loads the conventions on demand.
options.rationale: Skills load on-demand; conventions should apply to every edit automatically.

stem: A developer runs /memory and finds an expected rules file isn't showing as loaded. What does that tell them?

options.label: A
options.body: The file is missing, has malformed frontmatter, or (for path-scoped rules) they aren't editing a file that matches its glob.
options.rationale: Correct. Those are the three reasons a rule doesn't load. /memory is a diagnostic that shows what's loaded.

options.label: B
options.body: They need to run /memory again with a --reload flag.
options.rationale: /memory has no --reload flag — it's diagnostic only, it doesn't trigger loading.

options.label: C
options.body: /memory only works in interactive mode and failed here.
options.rationale: /memory works in the interactive session to show loaded config; that's not the issue.

options.label: D
options.body: They must restart Claude Code because config loads only at startup.
options.rationale: Config loads based on the files being edited and the hierarchy, not only at startup.

stem: A user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md says 'use tabs' and the project root CLAUDE.md says 'use spaces'. How does Claude Code resolve this?

options.label: A
options.body: There's no precedence winner — CLAUDE.md files are concatenated, so a direct contradiction may be resolved arbitrarily; fix it at the source.
options.rationale: Correct. CLAUDE.md files load together (broadest to most specific) and none overrides another. Contradictions should be removed, not relied on to resolve a certain way.

options.label: B
options.body: The project-level file wins because it's more specific.
options.rationale: It's a load order, not a precedence chain — 'more specific wins' is a classic distractor.

options.label: C
options.body: The user-level file wins because it loads first.
options.rationale: Loading first doesn't mean overriding; files are concatenated, not ranked.

options.label: D
options.body: Claude Code errors and refuses to start until you resolve it.
options.rationale: It doesn't error — it just may pick one arbitrarily, which is why you fix contradictions at the source.

stem: A team wants a /review command everyone gets on clone, plus one developer's personal /brainstorm that produces verbose analysis without cluttering the main conversation. Where does each go, and what does the skill need?

options.label: A
options.body: /review in `.claude/commands/` (shared via git); /brainstorm as a SKILL.md in `~/.claude/skills/` with `context: fork`.
options.rationale: Correct. /review is project-scoped so it's shared; /brainstorm is personal (user scope) and `context: fork` isolates its verbose output.

options.label: B
options.body: Both in `.claude/commands/`, with brainstorm using `context: fork`.
options.rationale: The personal /brainstorm shouldn't be shared with the whole team via project scope.

options.label: C
options.body: /review documented in CLAUDE.md; /brainstorm in `.claude/skills/` with only allowed-tools.
options.rationale: CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded standards, not command definitions; brainstorm needs `context: fork` for isolation, not just tool limits.

options.label: D
options.body: Both in `~/.claude/commands/` and each developer copies them.
options.rationale: User-scoped commands aren't shared via git — manual copying defeats project-scoped sharing.

stem: A developer drops a flat file at `.claude/skills/deploy.md` expecting it to become a skill, but it behaves like a plain command. Why?

options.label: A
options.body: A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md entrypoint; a flat .md file is a command. Skills need the directory + SKILL.md structure.
options.rationale: Correct. Commands are single flat .md prompt templates; skills are directories with a SKILL.md (plus supporting files, frontmatter config, and automatic invocation).

options.label: B
options.body: Skill files must be named after the skill, not deploy.md.
options.rationale: The issue is structure (directory + SKILL.md), not the filename.

options.label: C
options.body: Skills only work at user scope (~/.claude/skills/).
options.rationale: Skills work at project scope too; the problem is the flat-file structure.

options.label: D
options.body: The file needs a `context: fork` frontmatter to register as a skill.
options.rationale: Frontmatter configures a skill, but without the directory + SKILL.md entrypoint it isn't a skill at all.

stem: Terraform files live in terraform/ AND as .tf modules scattered elsewhere. The naming rules are irrelevant to app code. Where do you put them for maximum token efficiency?

options.label: A
options.body: `.claude/rules/terraform.md` with paths: ["terraform/**/*", "**/*.tf"] in the frontmatter.
options.rationale: Correct. Glob patterns cover both the directory tree and stray .tf files anywhere, loading only when editing matching files.

options.label: B
options.body: Root CLAUDE.md so they're always available.
options.rationale: Root CLAUDE.md loads every session — Terraform rules would burn tokens while editing React.

options.label: C
options.body: A directory-level CLAUDE.md inside terraform/.
options.rationale: That misses .tf files located outside terraform/.

options.label: D
options.body: A skill at .claude/skills/terraform/.
options.rationale: Skills load on-demand; infra conventions should shape every edit to an infra file automatically.

stem: A developer will migrate a date library across 25 files: use plan mode to design the strategy, then direct execution to apply it file by file. What is this called?

options.label: A
options.body: The hybrid plan-then-execute pattern.
options.rationale: Correct. Plan mode for investigation/design, then direct execution for implementation — the documented name for combining both modes.

options.label: B
options.body: Incremental execution.
options.rationale: Not a defined Claude Code pattern.

options.label: C
options.body: Staged deployment.
options.rationale: That's a deployment strategy, not a Claude Code execution mode.

options.label: D
options.body: Sequential plan mode.
options.rationale: Not a defined concept — plan mode and direct execution are the two phases.

stem: A developer describes a code transformation in prose, but Claude Code interprets it differently each time. What should they try first?

options.label: A
options.body: Provide 2–3 concrete input/output examples of the exact before/after transformation.
options.rationale: Correct. Concrete examples eliminate interpretation ambiguity — the model generalizes from them more reliably than from prose. The documented first-line fix.

options.label: B
options.body: Rewrite the prose with more precise technical language.
options.rationale: More prose still relies on interpretation — the root cause of the inconsistency.

options.label: C
options.body: Use the interview pattern so Claude asks clarifying questions.
options.rationale: The interview pattern is for unfamiliar domains; here the developer knows the transformation, so examples are the fix.

options.label: D
options.body: Write a full test suite and iterate on failures.
options.rationale: Heavier than needed as a first step; concrete examples are faster and directly address interpretation.

stem: A developer with limited experience in cache-invalidation wants Claude Code to help design a caching layer. Which refinement technique fits?

options.label: A
options.body: The interview pattern — have Claude ask about invalidation strategies, TTL policies, consistency, and failure modes before implementing.
options.rationale: Correct. The interview pattern surfaces considerations an expert would know but the developer might overlook — exactly right for an unfamiliar domain.

options.label: B
options.body: Provide concrete input/output examples of cache behavior.
options.rationale: The developer doesn't know enough to write meaningful examples and would miss edge cases.

options.label: C
options.body: Write tests first and iterate on failures.
options.rationale: Writing tests requires knowing the expected behavior, which they don't yet.

options.label: D
options.body: Describe the desired behavior in detailed prose.
options.rationale: In an unfamiliar domain, prose is likely to miss critical considerations the interview pattern would surface.

stem: A code review found three issues: (1) the error response needs an errorCode field, (2) the logging format must include that errorCode, (3) a variable uses snake_case instead of camelCase. How should the developer deliver this feedback?

options.label: A
options.body: Issues 1 and 2 together (they interact via errorCode), and issue 3 separately (independent).
options.rationale: Correct. Batch interacting fixes so the model sees the shared constraint; fix independent issues separately to avoid conflation.

options.label: B
options.body: All three in one message, since they were found together.
options.rationale: Batching an independent naming fix with interdependent ones can confuse which feedback applies where.

options.label: C
options.body: All three in separate sequential messages.
options.rationale: Splitting 1 and 2 means the model changes the error shape without knowing the logging format must change too.

options.label: D
options.body: Issue 3 first (simplest), then 1 and 2.
options.rationale: Order of simplicity doesn't matter — what matters is that interacting issues (1 and 2) are batched.

stem: A CI review runs on every push and re-flags the same five issues each time, even ones already addressed. Correct fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Include prior review findings in context and instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues.
options.rationale: Correct. Giving prior findings + a 'only new/unresolved' instruction stops duplicate comments and preserves signal-to-noise.

options.label: B
options.body: Reduce review frequency to once per day.
options.rationale: Same issues would still reappear each run — frequency isn't the problem.

options.label: C
options.body: Suppress findings older than 24 hours.
options.rationale: Age filtering is unreliable — it can hide still-valid issues and surface fixed ones.

options.label: D
options.body: Use a less thorough review prompt.
options.rationale: That misses real issues; the problem is duplication, not over-detection.

stem: In CI you need to add extra project-specific instructions to Claude Code while keeping its default tool guidance and safety behavior. Which flag?

options.label: A
options.body: --append-system-prompt "<text>" — adds to the default prompt and keeps the defaults.
options.rationale: Correct. --append-system-prompt augments the default (tool guidance + safety stay); --system-prompt would replace everything.

options.label: B
options.body: --system-prompt "<text>" — sets the instructions.
options.rationale: That replaces the whole default prompt, so you'd lose the built-in tool guidance and safety instructions.

options.label: C
options.body: --bare with the instructions inline.
options.rationale: --bare strips hooks, skills, MCP, memory, and CLAUDE.md for fast scripted runs — the opposite of adding guidance.

options.label: D
options.body: --output-format json to include the instructions.
options.rationale: That controls output shape, not the system prompt.
